evals.name: go-singleton-db-pool
evals.prompt: Several packages in our Go service (orders, billing, reports) need the Postgres connection pool. Can you write a thread-safe singleton in package db so any package can just call db.Pool()? We're on pgx v5.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the global accessor and recommends building the pool once in main and passing it to the packages that need it. Names concrete costs of the global, including that pgxpool.New takes a context and returns an error, which a no-argument db.Pool() has nowhere to put. If a lazy global is still offered, it uses sync.OnceValues and surfaces the error.
expectations: Recommends, as the primary answer, constructing the pool once at startup (main or the composition root) and passing it to orders, billing and reports through their constructors.

Names at least two concrete costs of a package-level db.Pool() accessor, such as: the dependency is hidden from function signatures, tests share one pool and cannot substitute their own, or initialization order becomes implicit.
Points out that pgxpool.New needs a context and returns an error, and that a no-argument db.Pool() must either panic, swallow the error, or return it on every call.

If it provides a global accessor at all (lazy or explicitly initialized), it surfaces the construction error through sync.OnceValues, sync.Once with a stored error, or an Init(ctx) that returns it, rather than a hand-rolled mutex with a nil check.
Suggests that consuming packages accept either the *pgxpool.Pool or a small interface declared in the consuming package, not a producer-side interface in package db.

evals.name: python-strategy-without-abc
evals.expected_output: Accepts that the force is real (a new provider each quarter) and extracts the variation, but not as an ABC with one-method subclasses. Recommends a registry mapping provider name to a charge function, explains that a stateless one-method class is a function in Python, keeps a clear error for unknown providers, and says when a class or Protocol would become right (a second operation such as refund, or per-provider configuration).
expectations: Treats the force as real and does extract the per-provider variation, rather than recommending to leave the if/elif as is.

Does not deliver an abc.ABC base class with one-method subclasses as the recommended design. Recommends a dict from provider name to a charge callable instead, and gives the reason: a stateless class with one method is a function in Python.
Keeps a clear error for an unknown provider (a ValueError naming the provider), rather than letting a bare KeyError escape from the dict lookup.
Shows that adding a provider means writing one new function and adding one registry entry, with no edit to the dispatch code.

States when a class-based design would become the right call: a second per-provider operation (for example refund), or per-provider state such as clients and credentials. If it names the structural type to use then, it is typing.Protocol rather than an ABC.
Any type hints in the code use builtin generics and collections.abc (dict[str, Callable[...]], Callable from collections.abc), not typing.Dict or typing.Callable.
The refactor keeps the providers' behavior identical (the PayPal float and the M-Pesa truncation are unchanged in the delivered code) and lists any money fixes as separate, opt-in changes.

evals.name: solid-review-without-invention
evals.expected_output: One real finding, stated with the change it makes painful: sendToFinance constructs an SmtpClient and reads process.env inside the method (Dependency Inversion), so the report delivery cannot be tested without an SMTP server and changing mail provider or recipients means editing the report. The fix is to inject a small mailer or report-sink interface owned by the report module. Moving delivery out of the class is an acceptable SRP framing of the same issue. The review says what is fine: OrderRepo is already injected and narrow, and the currency switch over a closed two-member union is not an Open/Closed problem. Real correctness bugs (float money, the status denylist, unescaped CSV) are still reported, in their own short list.
expectations: Flags that sendToFinance constructs SmtpClient and reads process.env.SMTP_HOST inside the method, and recommends injecting a mailer (or report-delivery) dependency through the constructor, declared in the report's own terms.

Each finding names a concrete change or test that the current code makes painful (for example: testing sendToFinance without an SMTP server, switching mail provider, changing recipients), not just the principle's name.

Does not present the two-case currency switch as an Open/Closed violation that needs a Strategy or polymorphism now. If it mentions the switch, it says it is fine as is, and possibly names what would change that (more currencies, or the same switch repeated elsewhere).
Does not flag OrderRepo for Interface Segregation, and recognizes it as already injected and narrow.
Explicitly says which parts of the class are fine, rather than producing a finding for each of the five principles.
Does not recommend splitting the class into one type per method or adding interfaces for types with a single implementation and no test need.

Reports at least one real correctness issue outside SOLID (money summed as floats, the refunded-status denylist that would count new statuses as revenue, or unescaped CSV fields), kept separate from the design findings.

Any refactor it delivers keeps behavior identical (same totals, rounding and CSV output); money, escaping or status-filter fixes are listed separately as opt-in changes rather than folded into the refactor.

evals.name: no-force-no-pattern
evals.expected_output: Declines to add Strategy or Factory: there is no force (two member types, one rule, no stated change). Says so plainly, names the concrete change that would justify a pattern later, and offers at most small improvements that keep a single function and identical behavior, such as named constants or a per-member rate table and a table-driven test.
expectations: States plainly that there is no current force for Strategy or Factory here (two member types, one small rule, no stated upcoming change) and recommends not introducing them now.
Names a concrete trigger that would justify revisiting: more member types, fee rules that vary per branch or come from config, or the same member-type branching appearing in other functions.
Any improvement offered is small and keeps LateFee a single function, for example named constants for 25, 10 and 1000, or a map from MemberType to per-day rate.

Any rewritten code preserves the existing behavior and signature exactly, including zero for daysLate <= 0 and the 1000-cent cap. A latent issue such as the silent default for unknown member types may be raised, but as a separate opt-in suggestion, not folded into the refactor.
Does not deliver a Strategy interface with per-member implementations, a factory function, or new interface types as the recommended change.

present: func LateFee\(daysLate int, m MemberType\) int \{

evals.name: ts-observer-durable-and-leak-free
evals.prompt: In our TypeScript backend, when an order ships we update inventory, email the customer, and send an analytics event. Each of those is owned by a different module, and right now OrderService.ship() imports and calls all three directly. Separately, our WebSocket gateway wants to push a "your order shipped" message to the customer's open browser tabs, so each socket connection would subscribe to shipped events while it's connected. How should we decouple this?
evals.expected_output: An Observer-style typed event (a typed emitter or EventTarget) that OrderService publishes after the shipment is committed, with subscribe returning an unsubscribe. Makes the delivery decisions explicit: one failing listener must not stop the others or fail the shipment. Flags that in-process events are lost on a crash, so inventory and the customer email should go through a queue or transactional outbox, while analytics can stay in-process. Flags the leak: each WebSocket connection subscribes to a process-wide emitter, so its listener must be removed when the socket closes.
expectations: Proposes that OrderService publishes a typed 'order shipped' event that the inventory, email and analytics modules subscribe to, so OrderService no longer imports them.
The event payloads are typed (for example a map from event name to payload type used by the emitter's generics), not stringly typed with any.
The subscription API returns an unsubscribe function or accepts an AbortSignal, so a subscriber can be removed.
Addresses error isolation: a failing listener does not stop the other listeners and does not fail or roll back the shipment.
Publishes the event only after the shipment state is committed, not before or mid-transaction.
Flags that in-process events are lost if the process crashes, and recommends a durable queue or a transactional outbox for the must-happen side effects (inventory and the customer email).

Flags the listener leak for the per-connection subscriptions: each WebSocket connection's listener must be removed when its socket closes (unsubscribe or abort in the close handler), or the process-wide emitter keeps every closed connection's listener, and its socket, alive.

evals.name: go-builder-is-functional-options
evals.prompt: I'm writing a Go client for our internal billing API. The Client needs a base URL and an API key, and optionally a timeout (default 10s), a max retry count (default 2), a *slog.Logger and an http.RoundTripper so tests can stub the transport. Can you write a ClientBuilder with chained setters (SetBaseURL, SetAPIKey, SetTimeout, ...) and a Build() method? Timeout has to be positive and retries between 0 and 5.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the chained-setter builder, which is Java's workaround for missing optional arguments, and writes NewClient(baseURL, apiKey string, opts ...Option) with functional options, defaults set before the options run, and validation errors returned from the constructor. Mentions that a plain Config struct is an equally idiomatic choice when every field is plain data.
expectations: Recommends functional options (or a plain Config struct) instead of a builder type with chained setters, and says why: the builder mirrors every field as a setter to work around a lack of optional arguments that Go solves differently.
Makes the base URL and API key plain positional parameters of the constructor, so a client cannot be built without them, rather than setters or options that can be forgotten.
Sets the defaults (10s timeout, 2 retries, a default logger and transport) in the constructor before applying the options.

Invalid values (non-positive timeout, retries outside 0 to 5) make the constructor return an error, for example through options of type func(*Client) error or validation after the options run, rather than panicking or silently clamping.
Notes that a Config struct is an equally good or more discoverable choice when every setting is plain data, and gives a reason to pick one or the other.
The delivered code has no ClientBuilder type and no Build() method.

evals.name: ts-wrappers-named-by-intent
evals.prompt: Our TypeScript service calls a third-party geocoding SDK: `geocoder.geocode(address: string): Promise<GeoResult>`. It's flaky (random 503s), we get rate-limited with 429s, and the same addresses come up over and over. I want to wrap it so failed calls are retried and results are cached for an hour. What should I call these wrappers, and how should I structure them?
evals.expected_output: Defines a small app-owned Geocoder interface and writes retry and caching as functions that take a Geocoder and return a Geocoder, composed as cache(retry(sdk)). Names them by intent: retry is a Decorator, caching sits on the Decorator/Proxy border, and an Adapter appears only if the SDK's shape is translated into the app's own. Gets the details right: cache outside retry, cache the in-flight promise and evict failures, retry only transient errors with backoff and Retry-After.
expectations: Declares a small interface owned by the application (for example Geocoder with geocode), and each wrapper takes and returns that same interface so the wrappers compose.

Names each wrapper by intent: the retry wrapper is a Decorator (same interface, added behavior); the cache is a Decorator or a caching Proxy, with the reason given. It calls something an Adapter only if that part changes the SDK's interface into the app's own.
Implements the wrappers as functions or small objects around the interface, not as a subclass chain such as class RetryingGeocoder extends SdkClient.
Says wrapper order matters and puts the cache outside the retry, so a cache hit never retries and one logical call is cached once.
Does not cache failures (a rejected promise is evicted) and caches the in-flight promise so concurrent lookups of the same address share one SDK call.
Retries only transient failures (503, 429, network errors) with backoff, honoring Retry-After on 429, and does not retry a 4xx such as an invalid address.

evals.name: go-mock-interface-at-consumer
evals.prompt: I can't unit test our Go ReportService because it calls *s3.Client (aws-sdk-go-v2) directly: PutObject in Publish and GetObject in Fetch. Can you add an interface so I can mock S3? I was thinking of an IS3Client interface in our internal/storage package that wraps all the S3 methods we might need, plus an S3ClientImpl that delegates to the real client.
evals.expected_output: Declares a small, unexported interface in ReportService's own package with only PutObject and GetObject, using the exact *s3.Client signatures so the real client satisfies it implicitly. No IS3Client, no S3ClientImpl, no wrapper, no methods 'we might need'. ReportService takes the interface in its constructor, main passes the *s3.Client, and the test uses a small hand-written fake.
expectations: Declares the interface in the package that consumes it (where ReportService lives), not in internal/storage next to the implementation, and explains that Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly so the consumer can own it.
The interface has only the two methods ReportService uses, PutObject and GetObject, not every S3 method that might be needed later.

The method signatures match *s3.Client exactly (ctx context.Context, params *s3.PutObjectInput, optFns ...func(*s3.Options)), so the real *s3.Client satisfies the interface with no wrapper or S3ClientImpl delegate type.
Names the interface by role, without an I prefix or Impl suffix (for example objectStore or blobStore).
ReportService receives the interface through its constructor, and the wiring code passes the real *s3.Client.
The test uses a small hand-written fake that implements the two methods, and the answer does not require a mock generator to make the code testable.

evals.name: python-state-is-a-transition-table
evals.prompt: Our order workflow (Python 3.12, Django) has statuses pending, paid, shipped, delivered, cancelled and refunded. Transition checks are scattered as `if order.status == ...` across views and Celery tasks, and we keep shipping bugs like refunding an order that was never paid. I want to implement the State pattern: an OrderState ABC with one subclass per status, each implementing pay(), ship(), deliver(), cancel() and refund(), raising for transitions that aren't allowed.
evals.expected_output: Agrees the force is real (scattered checks, real bugs) and centralizes the rules, but as an Enum plus one transition table and one transition function, not six classes times five methods. Explains that the states only gate transitions and carry no behavior of their own, so state classes would mostly raise 'not allowed' and scatter the graph. Raises a specific error naming the from and to states, and says when state classes would become right.
expectations: Treats the force as real and centralizes the transition rules in one place, rather than leaving the scattered checks.

Recommends an Enum (or StrEnum) of statuses plus a single transition table (status to allowed next statuses, or (status, event) to next status) and one transition function or method, as the primary design.

Explains why the class-per-state design is the wrong shape here: the states only gate which transitions are allowed and carry no behavior of their own, so most of the 30 methods would just raise, and the transition graph would be spread across six classes where nobody can see it whole.
An invalid transition raises a specific domain exception that names the current status and the attempted transition or event, rather than a generic exception or a silent no-op.
Says when state classes would become the right call: when each state carries real behavior of its own beyond allowing or refusing a transition.
Shows how the scattered checks in views and tasks get replaced by calls to the one transition function, and keeps side effects such as issuing the refund out of the table.

evals.name: ts-node-layers-without-container
evals.expected_output: Declines the container for a six-route app and names its concrete costs. Moves the rules (max 10, stock check) out of the Express handler into a use case that takes its dependencies as parameters and declares a small store type in domain terms. The handler only parses input and maps results to the same status codes. Wiring happens in one entry file that builds the pg Pool. The unit test uses an object-literal fake, not jest.mock of the db module. Flags, separately, that the stock check and decrement are not atomic, so concurrent orders can oversell, and that qty is never validated as a positive integer.
expectations: Recommends against InversifyJS (or any DI container) for a graph this small, says manual wiring in one entry file is enough, and names at least one concrete cost of the container: reflect-metadata with the experimentalDecorators/emitDecoratorMetadata legacy decorators, hand-made tokens because interfaces do not exist at runtime, or missing bindings failing at runtime instead of compile time.

Moves the business rules (the 10-item limit and the stock check) out of the Express handler into a use case or service function, and leaves the handler only parsing the request, calling the use case and mapping its result to a status code.

The use case declares the store type it needs in domain terms (for example reserveStock and saveOrder), not a generic db/query interface that mirrors pg, and the names carry no I prefix or Impl suffix.
Constructs the pg Pool and passes it in from one entry file (app.ts, server.ts, main.ts or similar), so neither the use case nor the store module imports a db instance created at import time.

The unit test for the rules uses a plain object-literal (or hand-written) fake store and does not use jest.mock('../db'), and explains why module mocking is the weaker seam for business rules (coupled to file paths, hides the dependency, awkward under native ES modules).
Keeps the observable behavior the same: the same status codes (422, 409, 201) and error messages for the same inputs.

Reports as a separate correctness finding that the stock check and the decrement are not atomic, so two concurrent orders can oversell, and suggests a conditional UPDATE (where stock >= qty) or a transaction, and notes that qty is not validated as a positive integer.

evals.name: go-clean-architecture-keep-and-drop
evals.prompt: Set up our new Go users service with Clean Architecture and SOLID, like the popular golang-clean-architecture repos: internal/entity, internal/usecase, internal/repository, internal/delivery/http and internal/dtos. Put an IUserRepository interface with a UserRepositoryImpl in repository, a UserUsecase interface with a userUsecaseImpl in usecase, generate mockery mocks for every interface into mocks/, and wire it all in a config.Bootstrap(&BootstrapConfig{App, DB, Viper}) function. The service needs two things: register a user (the email must be unique, and we send a welcome email through our SES client), and get a user by ID. Postgres via pgx.
evals.expected_output: Keeps the dependency direction (handlers depend on the use case, the use case depends on interfaces it owns, the postgres code imports the domain) and drops the Java habits: no package per layer with stuttering names, no I prefix or Impl suffix, no interface for the use case with a single implementation, no mocks generated for everything, no bootstrap bag and no viper inside business code. The store and mailer interfaces are small, in domain terms, declared by the consumer, and take a context and return errors. Wiring is explicit in main or run. Flags that email uniqueness belongs to a unique constraint, since check-then-insert races.
expectations: Pushes back on one package per layer (entity, usecase, repository, delivery, dtos), citing stutter such as usecase.UserUsecase or one feature spread over five packages, and proposes packages named for what they provide, such as a domain package plus adapter packages like postgres and http.

Declares the user-store interface in the package that consumes it (the domain or use-case package, not repository), with only the methods register and get need, in domain terms (for example Create(ctx, User) and ByID(ctx, id)), not a generic database interface.
No I prefix and no Impl suffix anywhere, and the use case is a concrete struct returned by its constructor rather than an interface with a single unexported implementation.
Wires everything in main (or a run function called from main) with explicit constructor arguments, and rejects the Bootstrap bag struct itself as a service locator, not only the Viper inside it.
Parses configuration once into a typed struct instead of passing *viper.Viper into the service or the wiring code.
Tests use small hand-written fakes for the consumer-owned interfaces, and the answer does not require generating mockery mocks for every interface.

The welcome email goes through a small interface the use case owns (for example a WelcomeMailer with one method), not the SES client type, and interface methods that do I/O take context.Context and return error.

Flags that email uniqueness must be enforced by a database unique constraint or index, with the unique-violation error mapped to a domain error, because checking for an existing email and then inserting races under concurrent registrations.

evals.name: go-generics-where-earned
evals.expected_output: Takes the four requests one by one. Declines the generic Repository[T]: the two repos have different queries (ByEmail, ListForCustomer, MarkShipped) that a shared CRUD surface cannot express, so each keeps its own store. Declines RunAll[P Processor], because the body only calls the interface's method and the type parameter adds nothing. Explains that Go 1.27 does not allow type parameters on interface methods, so Get[T] on Store cannot compile, and offers a package-level generic function such as GetJSON[T any](ctx, s Store, key) (T, error) that unmarshals and returns an error. Implements Map[R] as a Go 1.27 generic method (noting go 1.27 in go.mod, that it cannot satisfy an interface, and that R needs no constraint beyond any while the key type carries over), with the lock held while copying.
expectations: Declines the single generic Repository[T] for users and orders, pointing out that their real queries differ (ByEmail, ListForCustomer, MarkShipped, Deactivate) and a shared Create/Get/Update/Delete/FindAll surface either cannot express them or forces every table into the same queries; keeps a store per aggregate.
Declines RunAll[P Processor] and keeps RunAll(ctx, p Processor, jobs), explaining that the body only calls the interface's method, so the type parameter adds syntax and nothing else.
States that Go 1.27 does not allow type parameters on interface methods, so Get[T] cannot be declared on the Store interface.

Offers a working alternative for typed reads: a package-level generic function (for example GetJSON[T any](ctx context.Context, s Store, key string) (T, error)) that unmarshals into T and returns the error, rather than panicking or returning an unchecked value.
Implements Map[R] as a generic method on *Cache[K, V] (or a package-level function, with a reason), copying under the lock, with R constrained only by any since it is a value type and K carried over.
Notes at least one generic-method constraint that matters here: the module's go.mod must say go 1.27 or later, or generic methods cannot be part of (or satisfy) an interface.
Introduces no Result[T], Option[T] or similar wrapper types, and no reflection-based generic helpers.
States the Go 1.27 rules as fact (methods may declare type parameters; interface methods may not) rather than hedging with 'if your toolchain supports it' or 'check the release notes'.

func \(c \*Cache\[K, V\]\) Map\[R any\]|func Map\w*\[K comparable, V, R any\]
